forces: Orchestra with E♭ clarinet, bells and expanded percussion
intro: The finale of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14, “Songe d’une nuit du Sabbat”, depicts the artist’s funeral among witches and monsters, with the beloved’s theme given to the E♭ clarinet. Deep bells introduce the Dies irae, which is later combined with the witches’ dance.

sections.label: Intro · Muted string tremolos and calls
sections.mNote: High strings play tremolos above rising cello and bass figures.

sections.label: A · Idée fixe, E♭ clarinet
sections.mNote: Clarinet and E♭ clarinet play a distorted idée fixe

sections.label: Link · Bells sound C and G
sections.mNote: Bassoons and low strings diminuendo before the bells enter

sections.label: B · Dies irae in bassoons
sections.mNote: Four bassoons and two ophicleides play the funeral chant

sections.label: C · Witches’ round dance, lower strings
sections.mNote: Cellos, basses and violas begin an imitative dance.

sections.label: B + C · Horn calls, chant and dance
sections.mNote: Horn calls precede the two tunes, which are later combined

sections.label: Coda · Strings bowed, brass, C major
sections.mNote: The strings resume bowing; the orchestra ends in C major.

cues.title: Opening, muted upper strings
cues.text: Muted violins and violas play tremolo high above the cellos and basses, whose quick figures rise from the low register. Soft timpani strokes interrupt them. In Berlioz’s programme, the artist dreams that witches and monsters have gathered for his funeral.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 1–20, Michel Austin’s score transcription: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas5.pdf . Funeral gathering: Berlioz’s programme, part V, http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Idée fixe, E♭ clarinet
cues.text: The idée fixe returns in the clarinets, ornamented with trills and grace notes. After a first statement on C clarinet, the E♭ clarinet plays it as a fast dance. In Berlioz’s programme, the beloved has joined the sabbath.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 21–78, including the first C-clarinet glimpse and the later E♭-clarinet statement; Michel Austin’s score transcription and Berlioz’s programme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Humbert Ferrand, 1829
cues.text: On 2 February 1829 Berlioz told his friend Humbert Ferrand that “a descriptive symphony of Faust” was fermenting in his head, and that he meant it to strike the musical world with terror. In the finished symphony the link with Goethe’s Faust is in the last movement, which echoes the Walpurgis Night scene.
cues.evidence: Berlioz to Humbert Ferrand, 2 February 1829 (Correspondance générale no. 113), in Michel Austin’s translation; Austin on the Faustian last movement and Goethe’s Walpurgis Night: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm . Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 26: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/26

cues.title: Offstage bells on C and G
cues.text: Bassoons, cellos and basses fall to a long, soft note. Deep bells enter offstage, sounding C and G. Between their strokes the strings play fragments of the dance that follows.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 87–126, especially the offstage bell part from bar 102 and intervening string fragments; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 19–22.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dies irae, bassoons and ophicleides
cues.text: Four bassoons and two ophicleides play the Dies irae, the chant from the Mass for the Dead, in long notes moving together above the bells. Later statements shorten the note values and pass the tune to higher wind and brass instruments.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 127–221, headed Dies irae, begins with four bassoons and two ophicleides; later statements diminish the note values. Modern performances use tubas for the ophicleide parts. http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas5.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ronde du Sabbat, fugal string entries
cues.text: Cellos and double basses begin the witches’ round. Violas enter next, then violins, each group starting while the earlier players continue. The subject is built from quick rising notes and a turn.
cues.evidence: Movement V, Ronde du Sabbat from bar 241; successive string entries in Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 34–38.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Programme prefaces, 1845 and 1855
cues.text: In 1845 Berlioz required that the audience receive his programme before hearing the symphony. In 1855 he allowed the symphony to be performed without the explanation. In the later version the opium dream covers the whole work.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 and 1855 programme prefaces, and their differing placement of the opium dream: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Liszt at the première
cues.text: The day before the première, the nineteen-year-old Franz Liszt called on Berlioz, whom he had never met. Berlioz talked about Goethe’s Faust, which Liszt admitted he had not read; he soon came to love it as much as Berlioz did. At the concert Liszt applauded so loudly that the whole hall noticed him.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31 (Liszt’s visit on the eve of the concert, his applause, and the Bal, Marche au supplice and Sabbat making “une grande sensation”): https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/31 . Liszt was born on 22 October 1811: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Liszt

cues.title: Dies irae and Ronde du Sabbat combined
cues.text: From bar 414 the wind and brass hold the Dies irae in long notes while the strings play the witches’ round beneath it at speed. Berlioz names both tunes in the heading above the score.
cues.evidence: Movement V, combined Dies irae and Ronde du Sabbat from bar 414, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 59–64. The heading explicitly names both tunes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Col legno, violins and violas
cues.text: Late in the movement the violins and violas strike their strings with the wood of their bows: col legno. They play high repeated notes. Woodwinds trill above pizzicato cellos and basses.
cues.evidence: Movement V, bars 444–460, col legno in violins and violas; wind trills and pizzicato low strings in bars 448–459. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 64–66, and commentary at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final passage, C major ending
cues.text: The woodwinds play a short passage alone. The strings then return to bowing, fortissimo, joined by brass chords and timpani. The last pages move towards C major, and the full orchestra plays the closing chords.
cues.evidence: Movement V, final passage from bar 460: woodwind episode, arco fortissimo from bar 467 and C-major ending; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 66–76.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The E♭ clarinet takes the idée fixe
transitions.from: Intro · Muted string tremolos and calls
transitions.how: In bars 21–54 the slow chromatic introduction gives way to a brief clarinet statement of the idée fixe over quiet drums. An orchestral outburst interrupts it. The key signature changes to three flats, and the E♭ clarinet then plays the tune as a quick dance in E♭ major, with chords in the oboes and running figures in the bassoons.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 21–54; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 7–12, including the change to three flats and E♭-clarinet statement.

transitions.title: Low descent to the bells
transitions.to: Link · Bells sound C and G
transitions.how: The E♭-major episode breaks off. From bar 87 to bar 101, bassoons, cellos and double basses descend in long notes, falling to pianississimo. At bar 102, bells marked “behind the stage” begin tolling C and G, and the strings play short figures between the strokes.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 79–126, especially the low descending line at bars 87–101 and bells from bar 102; Michel Austin’s score transcription.

transitions.title: Bassoons follow the funeral bells
transitions.from: Link · Bells sound C and G
transitions.how: The C and G bells are followed by four bassoons and two ophicleides, which begin the Dies irae. They play the chant together in long notes, marked forte. High strings and woodwinds rest for this first statement.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 123–147, Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 22.

transitions.title: Cellos and basses begin the Ronde du Sabbat
transitions.to: C · Witches’ round dance, lower strings
transitions.how: An orchestral chord gives way to the Ronde du Sabbat in C major. Cellos and basses begin its quick rising figure, with a sharply accented turn at the top. Violas enter next, then violins, while the earlier parts continue to play.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 240–262, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 34–38: new key signature and successive string entries.

transitions.title: Horns return to the chant
transitions.from: C · Witches’ round dance, lower strings
transitions.to: B + C · Horn calls, chant and dance
transitions.how: In bars 347–379 the round ends on held notes in the strings and bassoons. Solo horns play the chant in short phrases, and divided violas begin to move beneath them. Solo cellos and a roll on the bass drum join the moving figures before the dance and the chant return together.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 347–379, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 52–53: horn phrases, divided violas, solo cellos and bass drum.

transitions.title: From col legno back to arco
transitions.from: B + C · Horn calls, chant and dance
transitions.to: Coda · Strings bowed, brass, C major
transitions.how: The strings play col legno, then stop for a short woodwind phrase. At bar 467 they return arco, fortissimo, against brass chords and timpani. Cellos and basses play the low notes with the bow again. The closing passage runs on to the final C-major chords.
transitions.evidence: Movement V, bars 460–524, especially arco at bar 467; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 66–76.

source.title: Berlioz, Songe d’une nuit du Sabbat — orchestral score
source.locator: Introduction, bars 1–20; idée fixe, bars 21–78; bells from bar 102; Dies irae from bar 127; witches’ round from bar 241; combined themes from bar 414; col legno, bars 444–460. The tuba symbol shows the two ophicleide parts; percussion includes the bells.

timeline.note: Muted upper strings tremble above rising cello and bass figures and soft timpani strokes.
A C clarinet plays the idée fixe over quiet drums; the strings join the crescendo.
The E♭ clarinet plays the beloved’s melody as a dance, with trills and grace notes.
Bassoons, cellos and basses descend and fade; deep bells toll C and G.
Four bassoons and two ophicleides play the Dies irae above the bells.
The chant passes through brass and woodwinds in successively shorter notes.
Cellos and basses begin the round; violas and violins enter in turn.
Woodwinds, brass and percussion join the strings’ imitative dance.
Horn calls sound over held bassoon and string notes; violas, cellos and bass drum begin the build-up.
Wind and brass carry the funeral chant while strings play the witches’ round.
Violins and violas strike with the wood of their bows; woodwinds trill above plucked bass notes.
The strings resume bowing; wind, brass and percussion join the final C-major rush.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and said that he was tired, so the boy did not have to explain his tears. Berlioz recorded the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt the flute and guitar, studied maps of distant islands and was deeply moved by the story of Virgil’s abandoned queen.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
